title: Neural Networks and Gradient Descent
oneLiner: Neurons, weights and activation functions, then how training actually works: a loss to minimise, gradients from backpropagation, and small steps downhill.
keyTakeaway: A neural network is layers of simple units, each computing a weighted sum of its inputs and passing it through a non-linear activation. Training measures how wrong the network is with a loss function, uses backpropagation to work out which direction each weight should move to reduce that loss, and takes a small step in that direction, over and over. The learning rate sets the step size: too small is slow, too large overshoots and can diverge.
explanation:
An artificial neuron is a very loose cartoon of a brain cell. It takes some numbers in, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up with a bias, and passes the total through an activation function. Without the activation, stacking layers would be pointless: a chain of weighted sums is still just one weighted sum, a straight-line model. The activation adds a bend. ReLU (zero for negative inputs, the input itself otherwise) is the common default for hidden layers; sigmoid squashes any number into 0 to 1, which suits a probability; tanh squashes into -1 to 1. Wire many neurons into layers, feed each layer's outputs to the next, and you have a network that can approximate very complicated functions. Its knowledge is entirely in the weights, which is why model sizes are quoted as parameter counts.

Training needs a single number that says how wrong the network is: the loss. For regression it is often mean squared error; for classification and for language models it is cross-entropy, which is small when the model gave high probability to the right answer. Training is the search for weights that make the loss small on the training data (while, as the previous lesson showed, still generalising).

Gradient descent is that search. Picture the loss as a landscape over all the weights; you are standing somewhere on it in fog. The gradient tells you which way is uphill and how steep it is, so you step the other way. The update is just weight = weight - learning rate × gradient. Backpropagation is the efficient way to compute the gradient for every weight at once: run the inputs forward to get the loss, then apply the chain rule backwards layer by layer, so each weight learns how much it contributed to the error. It costs roughly the same as a couple of forward passes, which is what makes training huge networks feasible.

In practice you do not compute the gradient over the whole dataset for each step. You shuffle the data and split it into mini-batches (say 32 to a few thousand examples); each batch gives a noisy but cheap estimate of the gradient and one weight update. That is stochastic gradient descent, and variants such as Adam adapt the step size per weight. One full pass over the training data is an epoch. Large language models are often trained for about one pass, or not much more, over an enormous dataset, while small models may need many epochs.

The demo is gradient descent on a one-weight loss curve, a deliberate simplification: a real network has millions or billions of weights and the landscape cannot be drawn. The curve has a shallow local minimum and a deeper global one. Try a tiny learning rate (crawls), a moderate one (settles), and a large one (bounces around or flies off). Starting point and step size decide which valley you end up in. The neuron playground above it lets you set two weights and a bias and see what each activation does to the output.
